title: Hi.
My name is Wojciech.
hero.lead: I live in Gdańsk and take an **AI-native** approach to my work. I build applications, tools, and experiments. Technology—software and hardware alike—has been part of my life since long before I got into software development. **I didn’t take the most direct route into the dev world, though.**

workflow.heading: Workflow in practice
workflow.intro: The process changes with the context, but it rests on the same basic assumptions. **I don’t reinvent the wheel unless I have to.** System design and implementation come later.

steps.title: Problem
steps.text: I start by understanding the user, the current workflow, the requirements, and the constraints before thinking about solutions.

steps.title: Research
steps.text: I review similar projects, libraries, APIs, and documentation. If I’m entering a new domain, research is also when I learn its basics and terminology.

steps.title: System model
steps.text: I define the architecture, the flows, the boundaries of responsibility, and the initial contracts. I choose the best-fit solutions, create the first version of the brief, and define the MVP scope.

steps.title: Implementation
steps.text: I make a plan, break down the first tasks, and start building. Both the brief and the plan may change when a working version reveals new problems or a better direction.

steps.title: Feedback loop
steps.text: Feedback comes from both automated checks and reviews of the working version. I use it to refine the implementation or adjust its direction.

example.label: The same process · a small example
example.title: This portfolio is being built with a similar workflow.
example.text: The scale is small, but the order of decisions remains similar. In this project, most subsequent iterations focus on content and information hierarchy.

steps.title: Research
steps.text: I spent several days reviewing hundreds of existing portfolios and personal websites, looking at conventions, layouts, visual styles, and ways of presenting myself and my projects.

steps.title: Problem/Idea
steps.text: The portfolio should show my projects and the way I work without pretending that I followed the classic “degree → junior → mid → senior” path. It should draw people in with a personal story, a considered approach, and rich project documentation—not with visual showmanship, technology logos, or inflated claims.

steps.title: Architecture and brief.md
steps.text: A lightweight, page-oriented architecture with a separate content layer in `.json`/`.mdx`, allowing content to evolve independently of the views. I also prepared an extensive project brief—with a particular focus on content in this case—based on a detailed context document that organizes information about me and serves as the source of truth for the entire portfolio.

steps.title: Stack and implementation
steps.text: A static website built with React and TypeScript, with libraries for rendering and processing longer `.mdx` content such as case studies and blog posts.

steps.title: Feedback loop
steps.text: Draft → plan → prototype → review → improvements, until the structure and direction are stable enough. New features, refinements, and content expansion all go through the same process.

timeline.heading: My path to software development
timeline.intro: My current way of working grew out of several earlier chapters: my first websites and scripts, years spent working in audio, a period in retail, and an intensive return to software development in 2024–2025.

items.title: Hosting, forums, CMSs, and my first scripts
items.text: Back in the days of yoyo.pl, I built my first HTML pages, sliced and modified templates, worked with CMSs, forums, and gaming servers. Joomla, Drupal, phpBB, and FTP/SSH, wrote simple Pawn and Lua scripts for San Andreas Multiplayer and AMX Mod X—mostly following tutorials and forum posts, using ready-made snippets, and experimenting a lot.

items.title: Music, audio and the technical side of production
items.text: I spent more than a decade working with music, recording, live sound, and multimedia. It was a separate path that gave me a strong technical foundation and fluency with tools. Many concepts used in software and AI—such as `sampling`, `bit depth`, `quantization`, `compression`, `buffer`, or `cache` — were already familiar to me from audio.

items.title: Seeing the process from the user’s side
items.text: Working in e-commerce, including order picking and delivery platforms, showed me how many software problems only become visible when you actually go through a process yourself.

items.title: Returning to development through generative AI
items.text: An intensive period of learning modern frontend and backend development, architecture, and agentic workflows. Since then, I’ve been regularly building my own applications.

statement.title: LLMs and agentic development.
statement.text:
Most of my attention is currently on LLMs and agentic development. I keep up with new models, coding agents, and the tools around them, but I’m even more interested in what happens one level above: how to choose tools, **how to design repositories that agents can navigate efficiently, and how to build feedback loops that let them verify changes independently**.

Many of these interests currently come together in **[RepoAtlas](/en/projects?caseStudy=repoatlas)**—a project I’m actively working on. As I build it, I’m also deepening my understanding of application architecture: `boundaries`, `dependency rules`, flows, module responsibilities, and ways to enforce these rules mechanically.
